pamphlet_excerpts: Orienteering First Aid: Orienteering is a physically demanding activity that takesplace over several kilometers of very mixed and often ruggedterrain (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 2: Hot weather may result in sunburn, heatstroke, heatexhaustion, and dehydration, while cold weather can lead to hypothermia and dehydration (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 3: In the hurry to be first, youmight stumble onto dangerous animals or poisonous plants (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 4: Before going out, spend a fewminutes reviewingpossible injuries and their treatment (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Orienteering First Aid): The best thing you can do to prevent injury is to be well-rested, well-fed, and physically fit before going out on an orienteeringcourse (p. 66).
Step 2 (Orienteering First Aid): A normal night's sleep and healthy meals will helpyou endure the rigors of the course and decrease the possibility of a physical or mental slip (p. 66).
Step 3 (Orienteering First Aid): If you are not physically fit, you may be particularly vulnerable to heat (p. 66).
Step 4 (Orienteering First Aid): Dehydration is caused by lack of water in the body (p. 66).

pamphlet_excerpts: Map Symbols and Topographic Features: Using a Topographic Map. maps you will find a number on it that tells its elevation abovesea level (p. 14).

Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 2: On orienteering maps, the index contour line does nothave an elevation number, but is thicker than the others and isused as a guide for the eye (p. 14).
Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 3: You can also "see" the shape of the terrain from the profile of the lines on the paper (p. 14).
Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 4: If a mountain is perfectly conicallike a wizard's hat, the contour lines depicting the mountain will look like a bull's-eye (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): Each contour line will be perfectlycircular, and all will be the same distance apart (p. 14).
Step 2 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): At one part of the mountain, the contour line may intersect a valley or a depression (p. 14).
Step 3 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): If thecontour line ran into the valley, it would lose elevation andwould no longer be considered the same contour line (p. 14).
Step 4 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): When a higher point like a ridge is encountered, the contour line will "V" downward (p. 14).

Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 2: Beginners' courses rely heavily on handrails to help thenovice get to each control (p. 41).
Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 3: The route for the easiest coursesmay actually go right down a trail or road, the handrail (p. 41).

Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 4: Collecting, Check-Off, and Catching Features Always look around and take note of the features you passas you move toward the next control (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): There may be someobvious features along the route, such as a large pond or smalllake, that will help send you in the right direction (p. 41).
Step 2 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): These arecollecting features, which lie between you and the control (p. 41).
Step 3 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): Equally important but less obvious are check-off features, which you will see along the way (p. 41).
Step 4 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): You can constantly verifyyour position by making a mental note as you pass the features and moving your thumb along the map (p. 41).
